extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and open-science policymakers interested in open peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic review and definition of the distinct traits that comprise 'open peer review' (OPR), with discussion of their presumed benefits, drawbacks, evidence, and examples across publishing platforms and disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and reviewers are aware of each other’s identity
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes conflicts of interest more apparent and increases transparency and accountability; theorized to encourage more thorough reviews and to enable review activities to be counted in career evaluation (measurement school). Potential downsides: reviewers may temper frank criticism to avoid offence, leading to poorer reviews; studies show mixed/no strong effects (existing evidence largely from medicine); may increase refusal rates and exacerbate delay/expense. Evidence-base is limited and discipline-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Review reports are published alongside the relevant article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishes full reports or summaries to make otherwise invisible scholarly information reusable, add quality-assurance (wider community scrutiny), incentivize reviewers by increasing visibility and enabling attribution (e.g., via ORCID/Publons), and provide exemplars for early-career reviewers (tone, length, formulation of criticism). Empirical findings mixed: associated with higher reviewer refusal and longer time to write reviews but not clearly with higher quality (van Rooyen et al.). Can increase transparency but may also increase delays or discourage reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider community to able to contribute to the review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called crowdsourced, community/public or public peer review. Can invite anyone (anonymous or registered) or require credentials (e.g., ORCID with publications). Aims to broaden reviewer pools (including industry, patients, interdisciplinary perspectives), reduce editorial-selection biases, and (in principle) improve reliability by increasing reviewer numbers. Criticisms: questions about commentators' qualifications, incentives to participate, and low uptake in practice (Nature experiment, ACP statistics). Modeling suggests public reviewers can outperform small expert groups only if sufficiently large (e.g., >50). More central in SSH than STEM due to transferability of narrative critique; likely best used as a complement rather than a substitute for solicited review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct reciprocal discussion between author(s) and reviewers, and/or between reviewers, is allowed and encouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables reviewers and authors to discuss difficult issues, fostering collaborative revision and consensus-building (examples: EMBO cross-peer review, eLife online consultations, Frontiers interactive collaboration stage). Theoretically improves communication and manuscript improvement; experimental/laboratory evidence sparse but suggests improved cooperation can enhance review accuracy (Leek et al.). Risks: requires more back-and-forth and editorial mediation, potentially increasing review time and costs. Evidence to judge overall effectiveness is limited and largely anecdotal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open pre-review manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts are made immediately available (e.g., via pre-print servers like arXiv) in advance of any formal peer review procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes posting to subject-specific preprint servers, institutional or general repositories, or publisher-hosted rapid-access platforms. Benefits: assertion of priority, faster public dissemination, potential for community feedback before formal publication, and possible improvement in initial submission quality. Enables overlay-review models and decoupled publication platforms (examples: arXiv, bioRxiv, Discrete Analysis, F1000Research, PeerJ Preprints, Open Peer Review Module for repositories). Can complement traditional review workflows; impact on overall review costs and quality varies by model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open final-version commenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Review or commenting on final 'version of record' publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication commentary channels (journal comment sections, blogs, academic social networks, Twitter, PubPeer, Retraction Watch). Treats peer review as ongoing: reputation of a work evolves through post-publication critique; enables rapid community-driven error detection (e.g., PubPeer critiques that led to prominent refutations). Uptake on publisher sites often low; much discussion occurs off-platform. Supports perpetual correction/updating models (e.g., 'living' publications) but does not by itself substitute for pre-publication selection/improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open platforms ("decoupled review")
rubrics_metrics.description: Review is facilitated by a different organizational entity than the venue of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes 'portable' or independent review services that organize reviews outside target journals (examples: RUBRIQ, Peerage of Science, Axios Review, overlay journals). Aims to reduce duplication of review effort (the 'waterfall' problem), accelerate matching to journals, and provide measurable reviewer outputs (Publons) or other incentives. Models vary (paid reviewers, discounts, platform-mediated reputational credit). Also covers overlay journals that perform only peer review while using repositories for dissemination. Effectiveness depends on adoption by journals and incentives for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliability and inconsistency (problem dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional peer review can be unreliable and inconsistent across reviews and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPR traits theorized to address this: open identities and open reports may encourage more thorough reviews via accountability; open participation and open final-version commenting may improve reliability by increasing reviewer numbers/diversity; open interaction could improve accuracy via cooperation. Empirical support is limited and discipline-dependent; no single trait resolves unreliability and some traits may have neutral or adverse effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and expense (problem dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can produce long delays and substantial costs in time and money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPR responses: open pre-review manuscripts reduce time to first public availability; open platforms can address duplicated review cycles across journals; open participation might reduce editorial costs in theory but often fails to attract sufficient reviewers in practice. Conversely, open identities/reports and open interaction may increase time and reviewer refusal, potentially exacerbating delay and expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of accountability and risks of subversion (problem dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional models can lack transparency and be vulnerable to subversion or undisclosed conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open identities and open reports increase transparency and make conflicts more visible, potentially increasing accountability. However, open participation could allow contributions from parties with conflicts, and where anonymity is possible (or retained), this may be problematic. Removing anonymity can also discourage critical judgments, particularly against high-status individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and publication biases (problem dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can reflect and reinforce social and publication biases (e.g., gender, status, affiliation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reports add scrutiny over decision-making processes; open identities remove anonymity safeguards traditionally used to counter social bias—though evidence that anonymity reduces bias is not strong. Double-blind review has been associated with some bias reductions in certain studies (e.g., increased representation of female authors), so trade-offs exist between transparency and bias mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of incentives (problem dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is often poorly incentivized and not formally recognized in career evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reports and open identities, together with platforms (e.g., Publons, ORCID integration), can make review activities visible and countable for career advancement and alternative metrics. Open participation might allow reviewers to choose work they prefer, but in practice it has not reliably increased reviewer engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wastefulness (problem dimension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much reviewer labour and useful critique remains invisible or unused after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reports mitigate waste by making reviews reusable and instructive (e.g., guiding early-career reviewers), exposing lingering reservations that accompany accepted articles, and enabling community re-use of review content. Decoupling review from publication and publishing review reports helps recover the scholarly value of reviewer effort.
